meta.title: Lesson 6 data: nine technologies, their key numbers and the three jobs
meta.license: Numbers from EIA and FERC are U.S. government works in the public domain; PJM numbers are quoted from a public PJM document; this file CC BY 4.0
meta.about: cf: annual capacity factor of U.S. utility-scale generators in 2025 (EIA, final): average output as a share of rated capacity, not the share of hours a plant runs. firm: the ELCC class rating PJM applies to a technology class in its 2028/2029 Base Residual Auction, the share of a resource's MW that PJM counts toward its adequacy requirement; one market and one auction, not a universal technology value, and an individual plant's accredited capacity can differ (PJM Manual 21B). A firm share is a planning rating, not output guaranteed in any particular hour. jobs: the lesson's reference sort, 'yes' (does this job well), 'partly' (depends on the plant, the place or the rules; either answer is accepted) or 'no'. For firm capacity the sort reads the class ratings: 'yes' at 60% or more, 'no' only for solar's 7% (fixed) and 10% (tracking), 'partly' in between or where ratings differ by place or plant; this cutoff is the lesson's teaching choice, not PJM's. Neutral wording: each reason states the evidence, not a preference.

jobs.label: Cheap energy
jobs.question: Can it fill the year with many MWh at a low running cost?

jobs.label: Firm capacity
jobs.question: Can the grid count on it in the riskiest hours of the year?
jobs.measure: Firm share: the part of its MW a grid credits toward its reliability needs

jobs.label: Flexibility
jobs.question: Can it raise or lower its output quickly when asked?
jobs.measure: [[ramp-rate|Ramp rate]], start-up time and how long it can keep going

tech.label: Nuclear
tech.how: Steam from the heat of splitting uranium spins a turbine.

why.energy: Output averaged 91.1% of its size in 2025, at a low running cost.
why.firm: PJM's class rating is 96%, the highest of any class.
why.flex: It can change output within limits, but U.S. plants mostly run flat out.

tech.label: Gas combined-cycle
tech.how: A gas turbine, plus a steam turbine driven by its hot exhaust.

why.energy: Output averaged 58.7% of its size in 2025; its running cost moves with the gas price.
why.firm: PJM's class rating is 78%: fuel on demand, though cold snaps can cut the gas supply.
why.flex: It follows demand within a [[ramp-rate|ramp limit]] and above a minimum output.

tech.label: Gas peaker
tech.how: A gas turbine on its own: quick to start, less efficient.
tech.firmNote: 79% with a second fuel on site

why.energy: Output averaged only 13.6% of its size in 2025: it costs too much to run for bulk energy.
why.firm: PJM's class rating is 67%, or 79% with a second fuel on site: there when called unless fuel or cold fails.
why.flex: Starts quickly and changes output fast, within its start-up, ramp and minimum-output limits.

tech.label: Wind
tech.how: Blades turn a generator; below rated speed, output rises roughly with the cube of the wind speed.

why.energy: No fuel: a 33.8% capacity factor in 2025 still adds up to many MWh at almost no running cost.
why.firm: PJM's class rating is 34% for onshore wind and 60% offshore: calm spells can fall on the riskiest hours.
why.flex: It turns down quickly, and can turn up again if it was held below what the wind allows.

tech.label: Solar
tech.how: Panels turn sunlight straight into electricity.

why.energy: No fuel: a 24.0% capacity factor in 2025, all of it in daylight.
why.firm: PJM's class rating is 7% for fixed panels and 10% with tracking: little output in the riskiest hours.
why.flex: It turns down quickly, and can turn up again if it was held below what the sun allows.

tech.label: Battery
tech.how: Stores electricity when it is plentiful and returns it later. Fully charged, a 4-hour battery runs at full power for four hours.

why.energy: It makes no energy: the U.S. fleet gave back 82% of what it took in (2019 data).
why.firm: PJM's class rating is 59% for 4 hours and 71% for 8 hours: it runs out if the peak lasts long.
why.flex: Switches between charging and discharging almost at once, within its MW limit.

tech.label: Hydro
tech.how: Falling water turns a turbine; a dam can hold water back.
tech.firmNote: plants without a reservoir; reservoir plants rated one by one

why.energy: No fuel: a 34.4% capacity factor in 2025, limited by the water that arrives.
why.firm: A reservoir can save water for the peak; river plants follow the flow (PJM class rating 35%); droughts cut both.
why.flex: Reservoir plants raise or lower output quickly; plants without one follow the river.

tech.label: Geothermal
tech.how: Steam or hot water from deep underground drives a turbine.

why.energy: Steady heat and no fuel to buy: a 65.9% capacity factor in 2025.
why.firm: Its heat does not depend on the weather, so it is usually available in the riskiest hours (no PJM class rating to quote).
why.flex: Usually runs steadily; some plants can follow demand within limits.

tech.label: Demand response
tech.how: Users agree to cut or shift their use when the grid asks.

why.energy: It makes no energy: users skip or shift some of their use.
why.firm: PJM's class rating is 91%: users commit to cut when called, within agreed limits.
why.flex: Quick to call, but each program limits how often and for how long.

steelman.title: Contested: can wind plus storage do the firm job?
steelman.about: The lull is computed from town_year.json (SPP's 2025 wind shape, thousandths of its best hour): the longest run of consecutive hours below lullThreshold, reported with its local dates (Central standard time). It is a stress case, not a battery size: the wind still makes some electricity, and the storage needed depends on demand, other supplies, equipment sizes and charging chances.
